prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

We wither, unlike stars; die, unlike hills and cisterns.Ana shadowed my protector, esteemed Arbad, who’s left us. But ana do not grieve; all sparrows exit the feast hall. Novelties don’t excite me, nor wyrdstaef affright me. Men are like encampments that soon become ruins. They come with their kin, leave only land behind when they go— the last herdsman rounding up the stragglers. Man’s a shooting star: light turned to ash. Wealth and kin a stain that soon wears away. The work we do inevitably gehrorene. The wise grasp this; the foolish fight it and lose. If my wyrd holds off a while, my fingers reach out for its stick.Ana can tell you stories, bent over the more ana try to straighten.Ana am like a battered sword that hasn’t gotten any less sharp. Don’t leave me! (The sparrow finds the exit suddenly—.) O you reproachful wifcynn: when the men go off Can your witchcraft tell us who’ll return? Do you faint because they flet ofgeāfon? You make everyone weep! for the burston bodies of the irreplaceable friends of your own youth. But neither the witches nor the necromancers know what the aelmihtig intends. Just ask them:Hwœr cōm the men? Hwœ﻿r cōm our protectors? They don’t even know when the rain storm will come!

prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: Ana, Arbad, But

outputs.L1:
We wither, unlike the stars; we die, unlike the hills and cisterns. Ana shadowed my protector, the esteemed Arbad, who has left us. Yet ana do not grieve; all sparrows must, in time, leave the feast hall. Novelties do not stir me, nor does wyrdstaef affright me. Men are like encampments that soon fall into ruin. They arrive with their kin and, when they depart, leave only land behind—the last herdsman rounding up the stragglers. Man is a shooting star: light turned to ash. Wealth and kin are but a stain that soon wears away. The work we do inevitably gehrorene. The wise understand this; the foolish resist it and are undone. If my wyrd holds off a while longer, my fingers reach out for its stick.

Ana can tell you stories, bent ever more crooked the harder ana try to straighten. Ana am like a battered sword that has grown no less sharp. Do not leave me! The sparrow finds the exit suddenly—

O you reproachful wifcynn: when the men go off, can your witchcraft tell us who will return? Do you faint because they flet ofgeāfon? You make everyone weep for the burston bodies of the irreplaceable friends of your own youth. Yet neither witches nor necromancers know what the aelmihtig intends. Ask them, then: Hwœr cōm the men? Hwœr cōm our protectors? They do not even know when the rainstorm will come.
outputs.L2:
We fade away, not like the stars; we perish, not like the hills or the cisterns.

I followed my guardian, honored Arbad, who has now departed from us. Yet I do not mourn: every sparrow eventually leaves the banquet hall. New things do not stir my interest, and fate’s rune does not terrify me. People are like camps that quickly fall into decay. They arrive among their families, but when they depart, they leave nothing behind except the ground itself—like the final herdsman gathering the last strays. A human life is a falling star: brightness ending in cinders. Riches and relatives are only marks that soon fade. All our labor is bound to collapse. The wise understand this; fools resist it and are defeated. If my fate delays a little longer, my hands still stretch toward its staff.

I can tell you tales that grow more crooked the harder I try to set them straight. I am like a damaged sword that has lost none of its edge.

Do not abandon me!  
(The sparrow suddenly discovers the way out—.)

O accusing women: when the men depart, can your sorcery reveal which ones will come back? Do you swoon because they have left the hall? You make all people cry over the broken bodies of the irreplaceable companions of your own youth. But neither witches nor those who speak with the dead know what the Almighty has planned. Ask them yourselves:

Where have the men gone?  
Where have our defenders gone?

They cannot even say when the rainstorm will arrive.
outputs.L3:
Human life is brief and passing, especially when set beside the enduring things of the world. The stars continue to burn in the heavens, the hills remain rooted in their ancient places, and even old cisterns may outlast the generations that built and used them. Against such permanence, people seem fragile and fleeting, appearing for a short time and then vanishing.

Yet grief is softened by the knowledge that death is not a fate reserved for one person alone. Everyone, no matter how beloved, powerful, or fortunate, must eventually leave life behind. This understanding does not erase sorrow, but it gives it measure. To mourn is natural, but to recognize the shared destiny of all humankind is to see loss as part of the order of existence.

Nor can people preserve themselves through wealth, family, or the works of their hands. Riches are scattered, kinship lines weaken or disappear, and buildings, monuments, and possessions decay despite every effort to protect them. What people create may endure for a while, but it too is subject to time. Nothing human is truly permanent.

Wisdom, then, lies in accepting fate with humility. The wise person understands that some things cannot be resisted or undone. Foolishness, by contrast, is found in struggling against what is inevitable, as though determination alone could defeat mortality, time, or divine will. Acceptance is not weakness; it is a clear-eyed recognition of the limits placed upon human life.

Even those who claim hidden knowledge cannot escape these limits. Neither witches nor necromancers can say with certainty who will return, who will be lost, or what the divine powers intend. The future remains veiled, and the purposes of heaven are beyond human command. In the end, people must live with uncertainty, endure loss, and submit to the mystery of fate.
outputs.L4:
The poem meditates on the fragility of human life and the certainty of death. It looks upon the world as a place where everything passes away: buildings fall into ruin, wealth fades, companions disappear, and even the strongest human hopes are worn down by time. Images of broken halls and abandoned places suggest that no earthly achievement can last forever. What once seemed permanent—power, treasure, friendship, and fame—eventually becomes silent and empty.

Against this background of decay, the text reflects on grief and uncertainty. Human life is compared to fleeting things: a sparrow briefly crossing a warm hall before vanishing back into the darkness, or a shooting star flashing for a moment and then disappearing. Such images emphasize how brief and mysterious existence is. People enter the world without knowing where they came from, endure suffering and loss, and then depart without understanding what lies beyond.

The speaker’s questions resemble the laments found in Old English poetry: Where have the rulers gone? Where are the joys of the hall? What has become of the treasures, the feasts, and the beloved companions? These questions remain unanswered, deepening the sense of sorrow. The poem does not offer easy comfort. Instead, it dwells on the pain of not knowing why people suffer or what destiny awaits them.

Even wisdom and learning are shown to have limits. A person may seek knowledge, practice magic, preserve memories, or search the past for meaning, but none of these can defeat death. Memory may keep traces of the dead alive for a while, yet it cannot restore them. Wealth may bring temporary honor, but it cannot protect anyone from decay. Human understanding reaches only so far before it meets silence.

In the end, the text suggests that mortality is the central truth of human existence. All people, whether powerful or humble, must face loss and uncertainty. Fate remains hidden, and the ultimate meaning of life and death lies beyond human grasp. The poem therefore presents a solemn vision of the human condition: people live briefly, love and suffer deeply, and seek answers they may never receive, standing before a divine or cosmic mystery that cannot be fully known.
outputs.L5:
Ana had always believed that every forgotten place had a story waiting to be heard. When she arrived in the ancient town of Arbad, she felt it immediately: the quiet streets, the weathered stone walls, and the wind moving through the narrow alleys all seemed to whisper secrets from long ago.

The people of Arbad were kind but reserved. They spoke little about the old tower on the hill, a place everyone avoided after sunset. Ana, however, was curious. She spent her days asking questions, reading faded records, and following clues hidden in the town’s history.

But curiosity can be powerful, and sometimes dangerous. One evening, as the sky turned deep purple, Ana climbed the hill toward the tower. Inside, she found not treasure, but a room filled with paintings of Arbad as it once was—bright, full of music, and alive with celebration.

Ana understood then that the town had not lost its beauty; it had only forgotten it. The next morning, she shared what she had discovered. Slowly, the people of Arbad began to remember their songs, their stories, and their pride.

And from that day on, Ana was no longer just a visitor. She became part of Arbad’s story.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a fragmented, archaic elegy in the voice of an old Anglo-Saxon warrior mourning a dead lord, blending Modern English with Old English words like “wyrd,” “Hwær cōm,” and “aelmihtig,” and using images of sparrows, ruins, stars, swords, and departing men.
counterfactuals.output:
**Elegy for the Ring-Giver**

Hwær cōm the gold-lord,  
the giver of swords?  
Hwær cōm the high seat,  
the horn in the hall?

Gone—  
as breath on the winter mere,  
as a sparrow through smoke,  
one wingbeat between storm and storm.

Wyrd hath taken him.

Now the benches are bare,  
the bright cups overturned;  
ash lies cold where laughter kindled,  
and the harp is hush’d  
beneath the hanging shield.

I, old in war,  
scarred with spear-memory,  
stand by the broken gate.  
The wall-stones weep with frost.  
Ruins keep counsel  
better than men.

O my lord, my light in battle,  
my shelter under sword-rain—  
thou art laid low,  
and thy thanes depart:  
one to the whale-road,  
one to the wolf-wood,  
one to the earth’s dark keeping.

Their footsteps fade.  
Their mail rings once—  
then no more.

Above, the stars burn stern,  
cold candles of the aelmihtig,  
watching this world’s waning.  
They saw our banners blaze;  
they see the ravens gather.

My sword is nicked.  
My hand is hollow.  
No ring warms it now.

Hwær cōm the oath-sworn band?  
Hwær cōm the feast and the fire?  
Hwær cōm the prince in his splendour?

All passes.  
Wyrd writes in iron.  
Men are sparrows, lords are dust,  
and halls—high halls—  
fall silent under stars.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose an experimental prose-poem that sounds like a corrupted translation of an Old English lament, with the speaker named Ana, references to a protector called Arbad, and themes of mortality, exile, fading kinship, and unknowable fate.
counterfactuals.output:
I am Ana, ash-name, after-speech, a woman or wound translated too many winters from the first tongue.

Once Arbad held the ring of shelter over us, broad-handed under storm, keeper of the hearth-oath, wolf-fender, bread-giver. His voice was a roof-beam. His gaze made the spears remember their iron manners. Where now is Arbad? Where the gold-clatter? Where the kin at the fire, the cup passing hand to hand like a small sun?

Gone: into earth’s dark grammar.

The hall stands with its ribs showing. Wind reads through it. Snow enters as if summoned by name. I sit beside the cold threshold and count not sheep, not stars, but the vanished: mother-brother, shield-friend, milk-sister, the boy who laughed with flour on his cheek, the old one who knew which herb unmakes fever. Their faces loosen in me. Kinship fades first at the edges, then at the mouth. Soon I shall not be able to say who was mine, only that there was warmth and it withdrew.

Exile is a road with no listener. I have worn it under my feet until my feet became road. I have crossed whale-road, bone-field, crow-meadow, the place where the black trees lean together and speak without vowels. Each land asks: whose are you? I answer: Ana. It says: not enough.

Night heaps its blue hides upon the world. The moon is a coin bitten by dead kings. In my sleep I hear Arbad calling from beneath the hill, or above the sea, or inside the locked room of my own breast. He says: endure. He says: all walls are loaned. He says: fate is a weaver with her face turned away.

But I do not know if it is Arbad.

Perhaps it is the raven making scripture of hunger. Perhaps it is the old gods coughing in their burials. Perhaps it is my blood remembering a house that no longer remembers me.

Mortality, yes—this is the lesson beaten into the shield: all flesh is frost-writing. The beloved body, warm and oath-bright, becomes soon enough a thing for roots to spell. The hand that gave, the hand that struck, the hand that touched my hair in the dusk: all go under. Even grief will go under. Even the word grief will lose its teeth.

Still I speak, though the tongue is broken. Still I bind these wrong words to the wind:

Ana was here. Ana wandered. Ana kept the ember beneath her cloak. Ana had kin, or dreamed kin. Ana had Arbad, protector, or invented him against the dark.

The sea answers in its old damaged language.

No man knows the end-shape. No woman lifts the veil from wyrd. The path runs forward wearing a fog-mask. We are driven, we are gathered, we are unmade. And somewhere beyond the last hill, perhaps, the hall is rebuilt of light; or else there is no hall, only snow falling perfectly on the names we failed to carry.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a dark medieval-style monologue about death and impermanence, mixing Biblical/Anglo-Saxon imagery with odd glitches and untranslated Old English phrases; include rhetorical questions beginning “Where are the men?” and “Where are our protectors?”
counterfactuals.output:
Where are the men? Where are the cup-bearers, the oath-givers, the wolf-helmed riders who laughed beneath rafters blackened by winter smoke? Their benches are empty. Their mead has soured in the horn. Their swords lie redless in the earth, and the earth remembers nothing.

Where are our protectors? Where are the ring-lords, the shield-fathers, the keepers of the gate? The gate hangs open. The hinge sings in the wind. The watchman is dust, the king is a name eaten by rain, and the banner has become a rag for crows.

Lo, all flesh is grass, and the grass is frost-bitten. A man rises like dawn over the fen and is gone like breath from a dead mouth. He builds a hall of oak, sets iron in the door, carves beasts into the beams, and says: *This shall endure.* But worm and weather answer him. *Hwæt.* The stone cracks. The beam rots. The hearth goes cold. The child forgets the father’s face.

I have seen the grave take the proud and the meek, the saint and the oath-breaker. I have heard the bell toll over kings, and over swineherds, and over nameless bones found under the field-wall. Dust unto dust, ash unto ash, and beneath the chapel floor the skull grins without rank or banner.

*Eala þu eorþe, ealra modor,* open thy black mouth. Take back the gold from the miser’s fist. Take back the teeth from the singer. Take back the hands from the builder, the eyes from the watcher, the tongue from the priest who cried mercy in Latin while the plague scratched at the door.

And what is glory? A candle in a crypt. What is beauty? A rose dropped into a charnel pit. What is strength? A spearshaft snapped under a horse’s corpse. The high hall becomes a fox-den. The churchyard swells. The sea gnaws the cliff where fathers are buried, and the bones fall shining into the foam.

The scripture says there is a time to be born and a time to die, but the dying hour is always nearer than we reckon. It sits at supper. It sleeps at the foot of the bed. It rides behind us with no hoof-sound. *Memento mori,* murmurs the monk, but his ink curdles—  
`[scriptorium_error: lamp//flicker//flicker]`  
and the letter of salvation crawls like a black beetle across the vellum.

*Ðær cwom deað, se deorc engel,* and no door barred him. He passed through iron, through prayer, through mother’s arms. He put his finger upon the infant, upon the bride, upon the warrior bright in mail. He said nothing. He needed no argument.

O ruined world, *middangeard læne is.* Loaned, not given. Borrowed, not owned. We clutch at it with corpse-hands before we are corpses. We count coins while our ribs are being numbered. We feast under the eye of the pit.

Listen: the wind in the tower is not wind. It is the whisper of those who asked for one more summer. It is the breath of kings beneath the mound. It is the answer to every boast:

All passes.  
All falls.  
All names are unmade.  
`[memory not found]`  
*Wyrd bið ful aræd.*
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: I want a pseudo–Old English elegiac passage inspired by “The Wanderer” and “The Seafarer,” but surreal and anachronistically broken: mention sparrows leaving a feast hall, women accused of witchcraft, dead companions, and the wise accepting wyrd.
counterfactuals.output:
Lo, I have heard in the frost-hushed night  
how sparrows flew from the feast-hall’s fire,  
small brown ghosts through the smoke-hole wan,  
leaving the benches, the bone-cups bright,  
the lordless laughter locked in horn.

The mead was sour. The harp had rust.  
On the wall a moon like a mailed shield hung,  
yet under it women were named for witches—  
wise-wives, herb-keepers, hearth-singers once—  
driven with ash-marks into the wind,  
while black birds wrote in the snow their runes.

Then spoke the sea, that sorrow-cold mother:  
“Come thou over the whale-road, wanderer lean;  
thy dead companions drink no more,  
their rings are earth, their oaths are rain,  
their mouths are filled with winter’s flour.”

I saw them still by the drowned mast standing,  
my shield-friends, pale in the salt-blue dusk,  
bidding me home to a hall that was broken,  
to a king that was dust, to a bed of stones.

Strange is the world: the wire sings in the marsh,  
iron stars fall where ravens feed,  
and clocks without priests count the doom of men.  
Yet the wise one sits with a weathered heart,  
holds fast no joy, curses no loss,  
but learns in the dark the old law’s word:

Wyrd bið ful aræd—  
fate is wholly wrought.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a literary pastiche of an Anglo-Saxon ubi sunt poem in modern English with scattered Old English vocabulary, featuring an aging speaker who compares humans to shooting stars, ruins, and a battered sword, and ends by saying no one knows what the Almighty intends.
counterfactuals.output:
**Ubi Sunt**

Hwær cwom the laughter under lamplight?  
Where are the hands that lifted the horn,  
the bright ones boasting in the mead-hall,  
gold-friends gathered, proud in their gear?  
The bench is bare. The black wind answers.  
Wyrd has unroofed the house of song.

I am old now, an eald mann,  
bone-cold at dawn, beard white with winter.  
I have watched the young flare over the world  
like shooting stars above the whale-road—  
swift was their shining, sweet was their falling,  
and night took back what night had lent.

So go men’s days: as meteors burning,  
as sparks from the smithy scattered in dark;  
a moment of glory, a glittering wound,  
then ash, then silence, then none to remember  
the name that once rang in the ring-giver’s hall.

I have seen stone cities slump into nettles,  
towers tooth-broken, gates gone to rust,  
the hearth-place hollow, the high seat empty,  
rain in the rafters, ravens nesting  
where queens once combed their yellow hair.  
Ruins speak softly: “Such is the eard  
of all who build beneath the clouds.”

And I am like a battered sword,  
edge nicked by years, ornament dimmed,  
hilt loosened, iron hungry with scars.  
Once I sang keenly in a strong hand;  
now I hang mute on the smoke-dark wall,  
remembering battle, awaiting the dust.

Hwær cwom the rider? Hwær cwom the feast?  
Where is the vow, the victor’s garland?  
The sea keeps secrets. The earth keeps bones.  
Snow covers footmarks; frost seals the furrow.  
Man passes over the middle-earth  
as breath on glass, as foam on water.

Therefore the wise one waits in sorrow,  
holds fast his heart, speaks few words,  
seeks some mercy beyond the storm.  
Yet of the ending, of joy or judgment,  
of why stars fall and strong halls perish—  
no one knows what the Almighty intends.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
